1	# Slash Commands — Complete Reference
2	
3	This document covers everything about slash commands: what they are, how Claude Code discovers them, the `$ARGUMENTS` system, Pinzo's four commands in detail, and how to create new commands for any project.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## What Are Slash Commands?
8	
9	Slash commands are `.md` files stored in `[project]/.claude/commands/`. When you type `/commandname` in Claude Code chat, it reads that file and executes its content as a prompt — with `$ARGUMENTS` replaced by whatever text follows the command name.
10	
11	They are project-scoped workflow shortcuts. Instead of writing out the same detailed instructions every time you want to build a feature or run a review, you write them once in a command file and invoke them in one line.
12	
13	### Example
14	
15	Without a slash command:
16	> "Build a complete feature for Pinzo. Read CLAUDE.md first. Check Prisma schema. Handle auth. Use Polaris v13. Add empty states and loading states. Include Toast feedback for every mutation. Run typecheck when done. Report what was changed."
17	
18	With a slash command:
19	> `/feature Add ZIP code import from CSV`
20	
21	Same instructions, one line.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## How Slash Commands Differ from Agents
26	
27	| | Agents | Slash Commands |
28	|-|--------|----------------|
29	| **Location** | `~/.claude/agents/` or `[project]/.claude/agents/` | `[project]/.claude/commands/` |
30	| **Scope** | Global or project | Project-only, always |
31	| **Invoked by** | Claude Code auto-routing, `@name`, SDK | You typing `/commandname` |
32	| **Has identity?** | Yes — name, model, description, persona | No — just instructions |
33	| **Purpose** | Specialist persona with persistent expertise | Repeatable workflow for one project |
34	| **Arguments?** | No — you describe the task in full | Yes — `$ARGUMENTS` placeholder |
35	| **Cost** | Uses agent's configured model | Uses current session model |
36	
37	**Rule of thumb:**
38	- Use agents when you need Claude Code to automatically know about a specialist (Rex, Koda, Vex, etc.)
39	- Use slash commands for project-specific workflows you run manually and repeatedly (build feature, fix bug, run migration)
40	
41	---
42	
43	## How Claude Code Discovers Slash Commands
44	
45	Claude Code scans `[project]/.claude/commands/` for `.md` files when the project is open. Each file's name (without `.md`) becomes the slash command name.
46	
47	```
48	Pinzo/.claude/commands/
49	  feature.md    →  /feature
50	  fix.md        →  /fix
51	  review.md     →  /review
52	  db.md         →  /db
53	```
54	
55	No registration needed. Create the file, and the command exists.
56	
57	📝 Commands are project-scoped. `/feature` in Pinzo is not available when you have Rankora open. Each project has its own `.claude/commands/` directory.
58	
59	📝 Command names are case-insensitive in practice but use lowercase by convention. Hyphens are fine: `/db-migrate`, `/release-notes`.
60	
61	---
62	
63	## The `$ARGUMENTS` Placeholder
64	
65	`$ARGUMENTS` is replaced by everything the user types after the command name.
66	
67	```
68	User types:  /feature Add CSV import for ZIP codes
69	$ARGUMENTS = "Add CSV import for ZIP codes"
70	```
71	
72	The replacement is literal — the entire string, exactly as typed, including spaces. Claude Code does not parse or split the arguments.
73	
74	### Using $ARGUMENTS in commands
75	
76	```markdown
77	Build a complete feature for this project: $ARGUMENTS
78	
79	Read CLAUDE.md first. Build all layers from DB to UI.
80	```
81	
82	When invoked as `/feature Add dark mode toggle`, the prompt becomes:
83	```
84	Build a complete feature for this project: Add dark mode toggle
85	
86	Read CLAUDE.md first. Build all layers from DB to UI.
87	```
88	
89	### Multiple uses of $ARGUMENTS
90	
91	You can use `$ARGUMENTS` multiple times in one file. Each occurrence is replaced with the same string.
92	
93	```markdown
94	## Task: $ARGUMENTS
95	
96	You are implementing: $ARGUMENTS
97	
98	Follow these steps...
99	```
100	
101	### Commands without $ARGUMENTS
102	
103	Some commands don't need arguments — they always do the same thing:
104	
105	```markdown
106	Run a complete pre-deploy quality review of all recently modified files.
107	
108	## Phase 1: Automated checks
109	Run npm run typecheck and npm run lint...
110	```
111	
112	Invoke as just: `/review`
113	
114	---
115	
116	## Pinzo's Four Commands
117	
118	Pinzo has the most complete slash command setup of any Boldteq project. These four commands cover the full development workflow.
119	
120	### `/feature` — Build a Complete Feature
121	
122	**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/feature.md`
123	
124	**When to use:** Any time you want to add new functionality to Pinzo. This is the most-used command.
125	
126	**What it does:**
127	1. Reads CLAUDE.md to understand the stack (React Router 7, Polaris v13, Prisma)
128	2. Reads 2+ existing route files to match code patterns exactly
129	3. Plans the feature (route type, models involved, data flow, billing gates)
130	4. Makes schema changes if needed (runs migrations)
131	5. Builds the route file with the correct auth pattern
132	6. Applies all Polaris v13 UI requirements (loading states, empty states, Toast feedback)
133	7. Runs `npm run typecheck` — zero tolerance for errors
134	8. Reports with file list, migration name, API endpoints, and test instructions
135	
136	It routes work to project agents based on what's needed:
137	- New admin page → **builder** agent
138	- New/modified public API → **widget-specialist** agent
139	- Both needed → spawns them in parallel
140	
141	**Usage:**
142	```
143	/feature Add product tagging to the admin dashboard
144	/feature Build a waitlist management page with bulk email notifications
145	/feature Add CSV import for ZIP codes with error reporting
146	/feature Create a delivery rules export as JSON
147	```
148	
149	⚠️ Be specific in your argument. "Add something to the dashboard" will produce worse results than "Add a paginated delivery rules table with sort by priority, bulk delete, and CSV export."
150	
151	---
152	
153	### `/fix` — Diagnose and Fix a Bug
154	
155	**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/fix.md`
156	
157	**When to use:** Any error — TypeScript errors, runtime crashes, wrong data, Shopify auth failures, Prisma errors, webhook failures, billing bugs.
158	
159	**What it does:**
160	1. Classifies the bug by category (auth, TypeScript, Polaris, DB, Shopify API, webhooks, billing)
161	2. Routes to the right agent based on category (bug-fixer for most, widget-specialist for widget/API issues)
162	3. Reads the full file where the error originates before touching anything
163	4. Makes the minimal, targeted fix — never refactors working code while fixing
164	5. Runs `npm run typecheck` to confirm zero errors
165	6. Reports root cause, files changed, and whether any follow-up is needed (migrations, env vars, etc.)
166	
167	The command knows Pinzo's most common bugs:
168	- Auth missing on admin routes (70% of Shopify bugs)
169	- Missing `where: { shop: session.shop }` on DB queries
170	- Polaris v13 prop changes (`status` → `tone` in Badge/Banner)
171	- React Router 7 imports from wrong package (must be `react-router`, not `@remix-run/react`)
172	- Prisma unique constraint violations
173	
174	**Usage:**
175	```
176	/fix TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined reading 'shop' in webhook handler
177	/fix npm run typecheck shows 3 errors in app/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx
178	/fix The widget returns 404 for shops with apostrophes in their domain name
179	/fix Subscription status not updating after Shopify billing webhook fires
180	```
181	
182	📝 Paste the exact error message as the argument. The more context the better. Stack traces, file names, and line numbers help a lot.
183	
184	---
185	
186	### `/review` — Quality Gate Before Shipping
187	
188	**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/review.md`
189	
190	**When to use:** After completing a feature or fix, before merging or deploying. This is the quality gate.
191	
192	**What it does** (5 phases):
193	
194	**Phase 1 — Automated checks:**
195	Runs `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint`. Reports results. Blocks the rest of the review if typecheck fails.
196	
197	**Phase 2 — Security audit:**
198	Checks for: auth missing on admin routes, cross-shop data leaks (queries without `where: { shop: session.shop }`), public routes with accidental admin auth, exposed secrets in API responses, unsanitized input on public endpoints, missing CORS headers.
199	
200	**Phase 3 — Shopify compliance:**
201	Checks for: Shopify API calls in components (must be in loaders/actions), raw fetch for Shopify API (must use `admin.graphql()`), missing idempotency in webhooks, raw HTML layout elements, missing loading/empty states/Toast feedback, ungated premium features.
202	
203	**Phase 4 — Code quality:**
204	Checks for: TypeScript `any`, `console.log` in production code, TODO/FIXME comments, hardcoded values, wrong Remix imports, missing error handling.
205	
206	**Phase 5 — API contract validation:**
207	If public APIs changed: verifies response shapes, status codes, CORS headers, and shop parameter validation.
208	
209	The review outputs a structured report with critical issues (must fix), quality issues (should fix), and a final recommendation: SHIP IT / FIX CRITICAL FIRST / NEEDS REWORK.
210	
211	**Usage:**
212	```
213	/review
214	/review src/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx
215	/review after adding the waitlist feature
216	```
217	
218	📝 `/review` with no arguments reviews all recently modified files (uses git diff). Pass a specific file to focus the review.
219	
220	---
221	
222	### `/db` — Database Workflows
223	
224	**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/db.md`
225	
226	**When to use:** Any time you need to change the Prisma schema, run migrations, optimize queries, or do bulk data operations.
227	
228	**What it does:**
229	- For schema changes: reads current schema, plans the change, adds fields/models, runs `prisma migrate dev`, runs `prisma generate`, updates TypeScript references, runs typecheck
230	- For query optimization: analyzes existing queries, adds indexes, applies select/include optimization, uses transactions for multi-step operations
231	- For data operations: applies correct patterns (`upsert` for singletons, `createMany` for bulk, `$transaction` for multi-step)
232	
233	It knows the full model catalog:
234	- **ZipCode** — `id, shop, zipCode, label, zone, message, eta, type` | unique: `[shop, zipCode]`
235	- **DeliveryRule** — `id, shop, name, zone, zipCodes, ...`
236	- **WaitlistEntry** — `id, shop, email, zipCode, status` | unique: `[shop, email, zipCode]`
237	- **WidgetConfig** — singleton per shop | unique: `shop`
238	- **Subscription** — singleton per shop | unique: `shop`
239	- **Session** — Shopify-managed, NEVER modify
240	
241	It also handles the SQLite (dev) vs PostgreSQL (prod) differences.
242	
243	**Usage:**
244	```
245	/db Add index on orders.shop for query performance
246	/db Add a notes field to WaitlistEntry
247	/db Create a new ProductTag model linked to shop
248	/db Optimize the zip code lookup query for high-volume stores
249	/db Add analytics tracking fields to Subscription
250	```
251	
252	⚠️ `/db` will NEVER run `prisma migrate reset` without explicit confirmation — this deletes all data. If you accidentally type it, the command will ask you to confirm and explain the consequences.
253	
254	---
255	
256	## Creating Slash Commands for Your Own Workflow
257	
258	### Step 1 — Understand what the command needs to do
259	
260	Write down in one sentence what this command's job is. "This command builds a complete feature for this project, handling all layers and quality gates." If you can't describe it in one sentence, it might need to be two commands.
261	
262	### Step 2 — Create the file
263	
264	```bash
265	touch "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/YourProject/.claude/commands/feature.md"
266	```
267	
268	The filename (without `.md`) is the command name.
269	
270	### Step 3 — Write the command
271	
272	```markdown
273	Build a complete feature for this project: $ARGUMENTS
274	
275	## Context
276	Read CLAUDE.md first to understand the stack and architecture.
277	Read at least 2 existing files that are similar to what you're building to match code patterns.
278	
279	## Process
280	1. Plan the feature (what files, what data, what APIs)
281	2. Make any schema changes first (if using a DB)
282	3. Build the implementation
283	4. Apply all quality standards (types, error handling, loading states)
284	5. Run the type checker — fix every error
285	6. Report: files changed, how to test, what to do next
286	
287	## Standards from CLAUDE.md apply. Read it before building.
288	```
289	
290	### Naming conventions
291	
292	- Lowercase only: `feature`, `fix`, `review`, `db`
293	- Hyphens for multi-word: `db-migrate`, `release-notes`, `type-check`
294	- Short: you type these often. `feature` not `build-complete-feature`
295	- One command per workflow: don't make `/feature-admin` and `/feature-api` separately — make one `/feature` that handles both
296	
297	### Best practices for command content
298	
299	**Always include:**
300	- What stack/framework this command is for (reference CLAUDE.md)
301	- Which agent to route to (if the command delegates to a specialist)
302	- What quality gates must pass before the task is "done"
303	- What the output/report format should be
304	
305	**The more specific, the better:**
306	```markdown
307	Bad:  Build a feature: $ARGUMENTS
308	Good: Build a complete Shopify admin page for: $ARGUMENTS
309	      - Use React Router 7 with Polaris v13
310	      - Include authenticate.admin in loader and action
311	      - Add SkeletonPage loading state
312	      - Add EmptyState for empty lists
313	      - Add Toast for every mutation
314	      - Run npm run typecheck — zero tolerance
315	```
316	
317	**Define "done" explicitly:**
318	The command should tell Claude Code exactly what state the code must be in before it reports completion. "Run the type checker and fix every error" is a quality gate. Without it, Claude might report done while there are still TypeScript errors.
319	
320	---
321	
322	## Creating Commands That Wrap Global Agents
323	
324	A powerful pattern: a slash command that provides project context to a global agent, so you don't have to type the context every time.
325	
326	### Why this is useful
327	
328	Without the pattern:
329	```
330	@sage Review src/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx. This is a Shopify app using React Router 7 and Polaris v13. Check for missing auth, cross-shop data leaks, Polaris v13 compliance, etc.
331	```
332	
333	With the pattern (a `/review` command that calls sage):
334	```
335	/review src/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx
336	```
337	
338	The command file provides all the Pinzo-specific context to Sage, so you only need to provide the specific file.
339	
340	### Template
341	
342	```markdown
343	<!-- .claude/commands/review.md -->
344	Review the following for this project: $ARGUMENTS
345	
346	## Project Context
347	This is the Pinzo Shopify app:
348	- Framework: React Router 7
349	- UI: Polaris v13
350	- Auth: authenticate.admin() from shopify.server.ts
351	- DB: Prisma with shop-scoped queries
352	
353	## What to review (route this to sage):
354	1. Security: auth missing, cross-shop leaks, exposed secrets
355	2. Shopify compliance: API calls in components, wrong imports
356	3. Polaris v13 compliance: loading states, empty states, Toast
357	4. TypeScript: no any, all functions typed
358	5. Code quality: error handling, console.logs, TODOs
359	
360	## Report format:
361	- Critical issues (must fix before shipping)
362	- Quality issues (should fix)
363	- Recommendation: SHIP IT / FIX CRITICAL / NEEDS REWORK
364	```
365	
366	### Examples for wrapping each global agent
367	
368	**`/quill` — generate copy with project context:**
369	```markdown
370	<!-- .claude/commands/quill.md -->
371	Generate content for this Shopify app: $ARGUMENTS
372	
373	## Project context for Quill:
374	- App name: Pinzo
375	- What it does: Shopify ZIP code delivery eligibility checker
376	- Tone: Clear, direct, conversion-focused
377	- Brand: Professional, reliable, merchant-friendly
378	
379	Write copy that matches this brand voice.
380	```
381	
382	**`/nova` — research with project focus:**
383	```markdown
384	<!-- .claude/commands/nova.md -->
385	Research this topic for Pinzo development: $ARGUMENTS
386	
387	## Context:
388	We're building Pinzo — a Shopify ZIP code delivery restriction app.
389	Focus research on: Shopify app ecosystem, merchant pain points, delivery use cases.
390	Return: competitive analysis, feature opportunities, pricing insights.
391	```
392	
393	---
394	
395	## Commands vs Agents: Decision Guide
396	
397	| Situation | Use |
398	|-----------|-----|
399	| You do the same workflow in this project more than once a week | Slash command |
400	| The workflow is always the same but the subject changes | Slash command with `$ARGUMENTS` |
401	| You need Claude Code to automatically route to a specialist | Agent |
402	| The specialist's expertise spans multiple projects | Global agent |
403	| The specialist is deeply tied to one project's code | Project agent |
404	| You want to invoke logic programmatically from Node code | Agent via SDK |
405	| You want to invoke it from the chat interface by typing | Slash command |
406	
407	When in doubt: create a slash command. They're easier to write and test than agents, and they're directly invocable by you without needing to describe the task in full every time.

1	# Agent Orchestration — Complete Reference
2	
3	This document covers everything about the Orchestration feature in Claude Hub: what it is, when to use it, how to build pipelines, the execution engine, advanced patterns, and troubleshooting.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## What Is Orchestration?
8	
9	Orchestration is a visual workflow system inside Claude Hub that lets you chain multiple Claude agents together as a directed graph (DAG). Each node in the graph runs one agent or custom step. The output of each node automatically flows into the next node as context.
10	
11	You define the pipeline once. Then you give it a top-level task and run it. Each agent handles one stage: researching, planning, building, reviewing. The whole pipeline executes without you manually passing output from one agent to the next.
12	
13	### The simplest possible orchestration
14	
15	```
16	[Task Input] → Nova (research) → Quill (draft)
17	```
18	
19	1. You type: "Write App Store listing for Pinzo"
20	2. Nova researches Pinzo and similar apps, returns competitor analysis and key angles
21	3. Quill receives Nova's research as context and writes the App Store listing using it
22	
23	Nova's output becomes Quill's input automatically. You didn't have to copy-paste anything.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## When to Use Orchestration vs Other Approaches
28	
29	| Situation | Best approach |
30	|-----------|--------------|
31	| Quick one-off task | Ask Claude Code directly in chat |
32	| Repeatable single-agent workflow | Slash command |
33	| Multi-step task with distinct specialist phases | Orchestration |
34	| Task where later stages need earlier stages' output | Orchestration |
35	| You want to test different pipeline structures | Orchestration |
36	| Programmatic agent calls from code | SDK (`callAgent`) |
37	| Interactive back-and-forth conversation | Claude Code chat |
38	
39	Orchestration is best when you have 2+ stages that require different expertise and where later stages genuinely benefit from earlier stages' output. If all stages can be done by one agent or don't need context from each other, use a slash command instead.

43	## How the Visual Canvas Works
44	
45	### Opening Orchestration
46	
47	1. Open http://localhost:3847
48	2. Click **Orchestration** in the left sidebar
49	
50	You land on the canvas. It has:

56	### Nodes
57	
58	Every pipeline is made of nodes. Each node represents one step.
59	
60	**Node types:**
61	
62	| Type | Description | Claude call? |
63	|------|-------------|-------------|
64	| Start / Task Input | The initial prompt. Pass-through — no agent runs. | No |
65	| Agent Node | Runs a global agent (Nova, Quill, Koda, etc.) with an optional instruction override | Yes |
66	| Custom Step | Runs Claude with instructions you write entirely yourself | Yes |
67	
68	**Node anatomy:**
69	- **Label** — the display name on the canvas (e.g., "Research", "Draft", "Polish")
70	- **Agent** (Agent nodes only) — which agent from `~/.claude/agents/` to use
71	- **Instructions** — what to tell this agent/step. This overrides or supplements the agent's default behavior for this specific step.
72	
73	### Edges
74	
75	Edges are arrows connecting nodes. They define the flow:
76	- Draw an arrow from Node A to Node B → Node B receives Node A's output as context
77	- Draw multiple arrows into Node B → Node B receives all upstream outputs, labeled by source
78	- A node with no incoming edges starts with the original task as its context
79	
80	### The DAG constraint
81	
82	The graph must be a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) — no cycles. You cannot connect Node C back to Node A if A → B → C. The execution engine uses topological sort, which requires no cycles. If you add a circular edge, the system rejects it.
83	
84	Valid graphs:
85	```
86	Linear:      A → B → C
87	Fan-out:     A → B
88	             A → C
89	Fan-in:      B → D
90	             C → D
91	Combined:    A → B → D → E
92	             A → C → D
93	```

97	## The Execution Engine
98	
99	### What happens when you click Run
100	
101	**Phase 1 — Graph validation:**
102	- Receives the node list and edge list from the frontend
103	- Builds a node map for fast lookup
104	- Detects cycles (rejects if found)
105	- Performs topological sort to determine execution order
106	- Ensures dependencies are respected (no node runs before its inputs are ready)
107	
108	**Phase 2 — Load agents:**
109	- Reads all `.md` files from `~/.claude/agents/`
110	- Reads `.md` files from each project's `.claude/agents/`
111	- Builds a map: agentName → full system prompt
112	
113	**Phase 3 — Sequential execution:**
114	
115	For each node in topological order:
116	
117	1. If it's a start/task node: store the original task as its output, emit `{ type: 'start' }` + `{ type: 'done' }` events, move on. No Claude call made.
118	
119	2. If it's an agent or custom node:
120	   - Emit `{ type: 'start', nodeId, label }` → the canvas shows this node as "running" (purple animation)
121	   - Collect outputs from all upstream nodes
122	   - Build context string:
123	     ```
124	     ## Output from [Upstream Node A label]:
125	     [Node A's output]
126	     
127	     ## Output from [Upstream Node B label]:
128	     [Node B's output]
129	     ```
130	   - Build full prompt:
131	     ```
132	     [Agent system prompt or custom instructions]
133	     
134	     ---
135	     
136	     [Context from upstream nodes]
137	     
138	     Provide your response:
139	     ```
140	   - Run `claude -p "[full prompt]"` as a subprocess
141	   - Wait for subprocess to complete (120-second timeout)
142	   - Store the output
143	   - Emit `{ type: 'done', nodeId, label, output }` → canvas shows green checkmark
144	
145	3. After all nodes: emit `{ type: 'complete', finalOutput }` → Run panel shows final result
146	
147	**Phase 4 — SSE streaming:**
148	
149	The frontend receives real-time updates via Server-Sent Events. The node statuses change live as execution proceeds:
150	- `idle` → gray (before run)
151	- `running` → animated purple (executing now)
152	- `done` → green with checkmark
153	- `error` → red with error icon

162

173	[Everything Nova returned]
174	
175	Provide your response:

314	## Node Instructions: Bad vs Good
315	
316	This is the most important thing to get right. Bad node instructions produce bad or empty output.
317	
318	### The root problem
319	
320	If node instructions say "analyze this" without specifying what to produce, Claude might:
321	- Ask clarifying questions instead of producing output
322	- Return a meta-commentary about what it would do, rather than doing it
323	- Produce the right content but buried in unnecessary explanation
324	
325	**Bad node instructions:**
326	```
327	Analyze the research and think about what content would work best.
328	```
329	Claude will describe what good content looks like, not write it.
330	
331	**Good node instructions:**
332	```
333	You are a Shopify app copywriter. Using the research provided:
334	1. Identify the top 3 user pain points mentioned
335	2. Write a 5-bullet feature list that directly addresses those pain points
336	3. Write a 150-word app description
337	
338	Return the bullets and description only. No commentary.
339	```
340	Claude has a clear role, a clear input, clear output requirements, and explicit format.
341	
342	### The explicit output format rule
343	
344	Every node instruction should specify:
345	1. **What format to return** ("Return a bullet list", "Return only the code", "Return a structured JSON object")
346	2. **What NOT to include** ("No commentary", "No preamble", "No explanation")
347	3. **Length or scope** ("150 words", "5 bullets", "complete implementation")
348	
349	Without these, agents often return meta-content (explaining what they're doing) rather than the deliverable itself.
350	
351	### More examples
352	
353	**Bad — Planner node:**
354	```
355	Think about the task and break it down.
356	```
357	
358	**Good — Planner node:**
359	```
360	Break the given task into 5 or fewer concrete implementation steps.
361	Number each step. Be specific: mention file names, method names, and data types where relevant.
362	Return the numbered list only.
363	```
364	
365	**Bad — Code reviewer:**
366	```
367	Review the code.
368	```
369	
370	**Good — Code reviewer:**
371	```
372	You are a TypeScript code reviewer.
373	Check for:
374	1. Missing type annotations
375	2. Unsafe type assertions or `any` usage
376	3. Unhandled promise rejections
377	4. Missing error boundaries
378	
379	Output format:
380	## Issues Found
381	- [severity: critical/warning] [file/line]: [problem] → [fix]
382	
383	## Verdict: PASS / NEEDS FIXES
384	```

420	## Advanced Patterns
421	
422	### Pattern 1: Fan-Out (Multi-Perspective Research)
423	
424	Use when you want multiple independent perspectives on the same topic before synthesizing.
425	
426	```
427	Task Input
428	  → Researcher A: "Find solutions in TypeScript/Node"
429	  → Researcher B: "Find solutions in Python approaches"
430	  → Synthesizer: "Compare approaches, recommend best for our stack"
431	  → Developer: "Implement the recommended approach"
432	```
433	
434	Both Researcher A and B receive only the task. Synthesizer receives both their outputs. Developer receives Synthesizer's recommendation.
435	
436	**When to use:** Architecture decisions, technical comparisons, multi-angle analysis.
437	
438	### Pattern 2: Plan → Implement → Validate
439	
440	A three-stage code generation pipeline.
441	
442	```
443	Task Input → Planner (Arya) → Developer (Koda) → Reviewer (Sage)
444	```
445	
446	Arya breaks the task into a build plan. Koda implements from the plan. Sage reviews Koda's implementation.
447	
448	**When to use:** Complex feature builds where you want architecture thought through before coding.
449	
450	### Pattern 3: Summarizer Nodes for Long Context
451	
452	Problem: Node 1 outputs 8KB of research. Node 2 outputs 12KB of code. Node 3 receives 20KB of context — slow, expensive, risks hitting limits.
453	
454	Solution: Add a Summarizer node between steps.
455	
456	```
457	Research → Summarizer (100 words max) → Developer
458	```
459	
460	Summarizer instruction:
461	```
462	Condense the above research into 5 key bullet points. 
463	Maximum 100 words total. 
464	Preserve the most actionable insights.
465	```
466	
467	The Developer then works with 100 words of targeted context instead of 8KB of raw research.
468	
469	### Pattern 4: Cascading Specialization
470	
471	```
472	Task (general) → Planner (breaks into sub-tasks) → Specialist A (sub-task 1) → Specialist B (sub-task 2) → Integrator (combines)
473	```
474	
475	Each specialist receives: the original task + Planner's output + their specific part to handle.
476	The Integrator receives: all specialist outputs and synthesizes them.
477	
478	**When to use:** Building multiple distinct components that need to work together. Example: "Build the pricing page" → Planner splits into (a) pricing logic, (b) UI layout, (c) copy. Koda handles logic and layout in parallel (conceptually). Quill handles copy. Final node integrates.
479	
480	### Pattern 5: Validation Gate
481	
482	```
483	Task → Developer → Validator → (done if valid, re-run with feedback if not)
484	```
485	
486	Validator instruction:
487	```
488	Review the code above. Check:
489	1. Does it compile? (TypeScript syntax check)
490	2. Does it follow the project patterns?
491	3. Are error handling and loading states present?
492	
493	Output:
494	## PASS / FAIL
495	If FAIL, list: [issue] → [required fix]
496	```
497	
498	If Validator outputs FAIL, you can see exactly what needs fixing and re-run with adjusted Developer instructions that address the Validator's feedback.

502	## Performance Considerations
503	
504	### Timing
505	
506	| Operation | Typical time |
507	|-----------|-------------|
508	| Start/Task node | < 1ms (no Claude call) |
509	| Simple agent step (short task) | 5–20 seconds |
510	| Complex agent step (full implementation) | 20–60 seconds |
511	| Full 3-node pipeline | 30–90 seconds |
512	| Full 5-node pipeline | 75–180 seconds |
513	
514	Every node makes exactly one `claude -p` subprocess call. Nodes execute sequentially — not in parallel.
515	
516	### How to keep pipelines fast
517	
518	1. **Limit context size** — use summarizer nodes between heavy output nodes
519	2. **Focused instructions** — specific instructions = faster, better output
520	3. **Appropriate agent for each step** — Sonnet is faster than Opus. Use Opus only for Arya/Sage/Rex nodes.
521	4. **Don't chain more nodes than needed** — 3–5 nodes is the sweet spot. 7+ nodes is usually overkill.
522	5. **Break into multiple smaller pipelines** — instead of one 8-node monster, run two 4-node pipelines sequentially
523

526	## Troubleshooting
527	
528	### Node turns red / error
529	
530	**Symptom:** A node shows a red error icon during a run.
531	
532	**Cause A — Timeout:** The node took longer than 120 seconds.
533	
534	Fix:
535	- Click the failed node to see the error message
536	- Simplify the instructions (break the task into smaller pieces)
537	- Or split the node into two nodes with focused responsibilities
538	
539	**Cause B — Claude CLI error:** The `claude` subprocess returned an error.
540	
541	Fix:
542	```bash
543	# Verify claude CLI works manually
544	claude -p "Say hello" --print
545	# If this fails, the CLI has a problem — re-authenticate:
546	claude login
547	```
548	
549	**Cause C — Empty output:** The node ran but returned nothing useful.
550	
551	Fix: The instructions likely don't direct Claude to produce a concrete deliverable. See "Node Instructions: Bad vs Good" above.
552	
553	---
554	
555	### Circular edge detected
556	
557	**Symptom:** System shows error "Circular dependency detected" when you try to run.
558	
559	**Cause:** You connected nodes in a way that creates a loop (A → B → C → A).
560	
561	**Fix:** Find and remove the circular edge. The system highlights the problematic edge in red. Delete it. Orchestration only supports DAGs (no cycles).
562	
563	---
564	
565	### Disconnected nodes
566	
567	**Symptom:** A node never runs — it stays gray after the run completes.
568	
569	**Cause:** The node has no incoming edges and is not a Start node. It's isolated from the graph.
570	
571	**Fix:** Connect the node to at least one other node. Either draw an edge from a preceding node to it, or delete it if it's not needed.
572	
573	---
574	
575	### Output is meta-commentary instead of content
576	
577	**Symptom:** A node returns "I would write the listing like this: [description of the listing]" instead of the actual listing.
578	
579	**Cause:** Node instructions don't specify that the agent should produce the deliverable directly.
580	
581	**Fix:** Add explicit output format instructions:
582	```
583	Write the listing. Return the listing only. No preamble, no commentary, no explanation.
584	```
585	
586	See "Node Instructions: Bad vs Good" for more examples.
587	
588	---
589	
590	### Context ballooning (slow pipeline)
591	
592	**Symptom:** Later nodes in the pipeline are very slow or timing out.
593	
594	**Cause:** Upstream nodes produced large outputs that all get passed as context to downstream nodes. By node 4 or 5, the context is 20KB+ of text.
595	
596	**Fix:** Add a Summarizer node:
597	```
598	Node 3 (long output) → Summarizer ("Condense to 5 key points, max 200 words") → Node 4
599	```
600	
601	---
602	
603	### Save not persisting
604	
605	**Symptom:** You save a pipeline, close Claude Hub, reopen it, and the pipeline is gone.
606	
607	**Cause:** Write permission issue on `orchestrations.json`.
608	
609	**Fix:**
610	```bash
611	ls -l "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/orchestrations.json"
612	# If not writable:
613	chmod 644 "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/orchestrations.json"
614	```
615

617	
618	### SSE events not streaming (run panel shows nothing)
619	
620	**Symptom:** You click Run, nothing happens in the run panel. After a long wait, maybe an error appears.
621	
622	**Cause:** The SSE connection between the frontend and backend is broken. Often caused by a proxy or browser extension interrupting the connection.
623	
624	**Fix:**
625	1. Check Claude Hub logs: `pm2 logs claude-hub --lines 30`
626	2. Look for errors in the browser console (F12 → Console)
627	3. Try a hard reload: Cmd+Shift+R
628	4. If pm2 shows errors: `pm2 restart claude-hub` then reload the page

2	
3	This guide covers everything you need to do when starting a new project or onboarding an existing one. By the end, Claude Code will know about the project, your agents will have context, slash commands will be available, and the SDK will be wired up.

6	
7	## Why Setup Matters
8	
9	A new project without proper setup means:
10	- Claude Code has no knowledge of the stack, patterns, or decisions
11	- No repeatable commands — you re-explain the same workflow every session
12	- No SDK access — you can't call agents programmatically
13	- Claude Hub doesn't know the project exists — no dashboard, no agent management
14	
15	A properly setup project means:
16	- Claude Code opens with full context on the first message
17	- `/feature`, `/fix`, `/review` work immediately
18	- `callAgent('koda', 'build X')` works from any script
19	- The project appears in Claude Hub with all agents and commands visible

22	
23	## Step 1 — Create the Project's CLAUDE.md
24	
25	### Why this matters
26	
27	The project-level `CLAUDE.md` at the project root is read by Claude Code when that project is open. It supplements the global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` with project-specific context: exact stack versions, folder structure, architecture decisions, and patterns specific to this codebase.
28	
29	Without it, Claude Code builds on generic assumptions. With it, Claude Code knows exactly what `authenticate.admin(request)` means, what your Prisma models look like, and what your quality standards are.
30

33	Every project CLAUDE.md must have:

40	- UI: [UI library and version]
41	- Auth: [how auth works]
42	- Database: [ORM + DB]
43	- Language: TypeScript everywhere — zero plain .js files
44	- Bundler: [if applicable]
45	- Node: [minimum version]
46

49	[Show the actual top-level directories and key files]
50	\`\`\`
51

60	
61	## Database Models

63	
64	## Route Patterns
65	[If using file-based routing — show the pattern table]
66	
67	## Quality Gates
68	[What must pass before any code is considered done]

70	- [project-specific checks]

# Slash Commands

## What They Are

Slash commands are `.md` files stored in `.claude/commands/`. When you type `/commandname` in Claude Code chat, it reads that file and runs its content as a prompt — with `$ARGUMENTS` replaced by whatever text follows the command name.

**You invoke commands. Claude invokes agents.**

- You type `/feature Add dark mode` → Claude Code reads `feature.md`, runs it
- Claude decides to use `@koda` → Claude invokes the agent automatically
- Commands are manual, typed shortcuts. Agents are automatic, routed specialists.

---

## Command Scopes

| Scope | Location | Available when |
|-------|----------|---------------|
| Global | `~/.claude/commands/*.md` | Any project is open |
| Project | `YourProject/.claude/commands/*.md` | That specific project is open |

No registration needed. Create the file — the command exists.

```
Pinzo/.claude/commands/
  feature.md    →  /feature
  fix.md        →  /fix
  review.md     →  /review
  db.md         →  /db
```

---

## The `$ARGUMENTS` Placeholder

`$ARGUMENTS` is replaced by everything you type after the command name.

```
You type:    /feature Add ZIP code import from CSV
$ARGUMENTS = "Add ZIP code import from CSV"
```

- Replacement is literal — the entire string, exactly as typed
- Use `$ARGUMENTS` multiple times in one file — each instance gets the same value
- Commands without `$ARGUMENTS` are always invoked as `/commandname` with no args

---

## File Format

Plain markdown. No frontmatter. No special syntax beyond `$ARGUMENTS`.

```markdown
Build a complete feature for this project: $ARGUMENTS

## Before starting
Read CLAUDE.md at the project root. Understand the stack and conventions.

## Process
1. Read 2+ existing files that are similar to match code patterns
2. Plan: what files, what DB changes, what APIs, what UI
3. Make schema changes first if needed, run migrations
4. Build the implementation following all CLAUDE.md patterns
5. Run npm run typecheck — zero tolerance for errors

## Report when done
- Files created/modified (with paths)
- DB changes (migration name or "none")
- How to test (step by step)
```

---

## Standard Commands — Full Content

### `/commit` — Stage, write commit message, commit

```markdown
Stage all modified files and create a git commit for this project.

## Process
1. Run: git status — review what changed
2. Run: git diff --staged — understand the actual changes
3. Stage all relevant files: git add [files] (never git add . blindly)
4. Write a commit message that:
   - First line: imperative, under 72 chars ("Add ZIP code CSV import")
   - Body (if needed): what changed and why, not how
5. Commit: git commit -m "[message]"
6. Report: commit hash, message, files included

## Rules
- Never commit .env files or secrets
- Never commit node_modules
- Never use --no-verify
- If typecheck fails, fix it first — don't commit broken code
```

### `/review` — Quality gate before shipping

```markdown
Review the most recent changes in this project: $ARGUMENTS

## Phase 1 — Automated checks
Run:
1. npm run typecheck — report PASS or FAIL with error count
2. npm run lint — report PASS or FAIL

If typecheck FAILS: stop here. Do not proceed until errors are fixed.

## Phase 2 — Security audit
Check for:
- Missing authentication on protected routes
- User data accessible without authorization check
- Input validation missing on API endpoints
- Hardcoded secrets or API keys in source
- Sensitive data exposed in API responses

## Phase 3 — Code quality
Check for:
- TypeScript `any` or unsafe type assertions
- Missing error handling on async operations
- console.log left in production code
- Missing loading/empty/error states in UI
- TODO/FIXME comments left in shipped code

## Output format
### Automated Checks
- TypeCheck: PASS/FAIL
- Lint: PASS/FAIL

### Critical Issues (Must Fix Before Shipping)
[numbered list — file:line, problem, fix]

### Quality Issues (Should Fix)
[numbered list]

### Recommendation: SHIP IT / FIX CRITICAL FIRST / NEEDS REWORK
```

### `/train` — Extract lessons to memory brain

```markdown
Extract lessons from this session and update the memory brain.

Route this to @mira.

## What to extract
1. Patterns that worked well — save to ~/.claude/memory/patterns/good/
2. Antipatterns discovered — save to ~/.claude/memory/patterns/avoid/antipatterns.md
3. Project-specific lessons — save to ~/.claude/memory/projects/[project-slug].md
4. Stack-specific insights — save to ~/.claude/memory/stacks/[stack].md
5. Update ~/.claude/memory/MEMORY.md index if new files were created

## Format for each lesson
- What happened
- Why it matters
- The rule going forward (one sentence, actionable)

## Report
- Files updated (with paths)
- Number of lessons captured
- Any lessons that couldn't be categorized
```

### `/deploy` — Pre-deploy checklist and deployment

```markdown
Run pre-deploy checks and deploy this project: $ARGUMENTS

Route this to @bolt.

## Pre-deploy checklist (ALL must pass)
1. npm run typecheck — zero errors
2. npm run lint — zero errors
3. npm run build — must succeed with no warnings
4. Check .env.example matches actual .env keys (no missing vars)
5. Check no console.logs in production paths
6. Check no TODO/FIXME in recently changed files
7. Review git log — confirm only intended commits are included

## Deploy
Target environment: $ARGUMENTS (default: production)

Follow the project's deploy instructions in CLAUDE.md.
For Vercel: vercel --prod
For Railway: railway up

## Post-deploy
- Verify the deploy URL responds (HTTP 200)
- Test one critical user flow end-to-end
- Report: deploy URL, deploy time, any warnings
```

### `/fix` — Debug and fix any issue

```markdown
Fix this issue: $ARGUMENTS

## Debugging process
1. Read the FULL file where the error originates — understand context before touching anything
2. Run npm run typecheck to see all TypeScript errors at once
3. Identify the root cause — not the symptom
4. Make the minimal, targeted fix — never refactor working code while fixing a bug
5. Run npm run typecheck again — confirm zero errors

## Rules
- Fix ONLY what is broken
- Never use // @ts-ignore or `as any` — fix the root cause
- Make the smallest change that resolves the issue
- If the fix requires a DB migration, run it

## Report
- Root cause (1 sentence)
- Files changed (file:line_range for each change)
- Fix applied (what changed and why)
- Verification: npm run typecheck — 0 errors
```

### `/feature` — Plan and build a complete feature

```markdown
Build a complete feature for this project: $ARGUMENTS

## Before starting
1. Read CLAUDE.md at the project root — understand the exact stack and rules
2. Read 2+ existing files similar to what you're building — match code patterns exactly

## Build order
1. Types — TypeScript interfaces/types for this feature
2. Database — schema changes + migration (if needed)
3. API — routes/actions with Zod validation + auth check
4. UI — components, pages, forms with loading/empty/error states
5. Integration — wire everything together

## Quality gates (ALL must pass before reporting done)
- npm run typecheck — zero errors
- Every API route validates input with Zod
- Every async operation has error handling
- Every list view has an empty state
- Every form mutation has user feedback (Toast or equivalent)
- Every async UI has a loading state

## Report
- Files created/modified (with absolute paths)
- DB changes (migration name or "none")
- API endpoints (method + path + params)
- How to test (step by step)
```

---

## Creating Commands

### Via Claude Hub UI

1. Open `http://localhost:3847`
2. Navigate to a project → **Commands** tab
3. Click **New Command**
4. Enter the command name (becomes the filename, no `.md`)
5. Write the content
6. Save

### Manually

```bash

# Orchestration

## What It Is

Orchestration is a visual DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) builder in Claude Hub. You chain multiple agents into a pipeline. Each node runs one agent. The output of each node flows automatically into the next node as context.

You define the pipeline once. Give it a task. Every stage runs in sequence without you manually passing output between agents.

**Simplest example:**

```
[Task Input] → Nova (research) → Quill (draft)
```

You type "Write App Store listing for Pinzo." Nova researches competitors and angles. Quill receives Nova's full output as context and writes the listing. You didn't copy-paste anything.

---

## When to Use Orchestration

| Situation | Use instead |
|-----------|-------------|
| Quick one-off task | Claude Code chat |
| Repeatable single-agent workflow | Slash command |
| Multi-step task requiring distinct specialist phases | **Orchestration** |
| Later stages need earlier stages' output | **Orchestration** |
| Programmatic agent calls from code | SDK (`callAgent`) |

Orchestration shines when you have 2+ stages with different expertise where later stages genuinely benefit from earlier stages' output.

---

## The Canvas

Open: `http://localhost:3847` → **Orchestration** in the left sidebar.

**Canvas layout:**
- Main canvas area — drag and position nodes
- Right sidebar — configure selected node
- Bottom panel — Run panel (task input, live log, final output)
- Top toolbar — New, Save, template picker, node palette

---

## Node Types

| Type | Claude call? | Description |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| Start / Task Input | No | Entry point. Passes your task text as output. Free — no API cost. |
| Agent Node | Yes | Runs a global agent (`~/.claude/agents/`) with optional instruction override |
| Custom Step | Yes | Runs Claude with instructions you write entirely yourself |

**Node anatomy:**
- **Label** — display name on canvas ("Research", "Draft", "Validate")
- **Agent** (Agent nodes) — which agent to use
- **Instructions** — what to tell this agent for this specific step

---

## Edges (Connections)

- Draw arrow from Node A to Node B → Node B receives Node A's output as context
- Multiple arrows into one node → that node receives all upstream outputs, labeled by source
- No cycles allowed — the graph must be a DAG

**Valid graph shapes:**

```
Linear:   A → B → C
Fan-out:  A → B
          A → C
Fan-in:   B → D
          C → D
Combined: A → B → D → E
          A → C → D
```

---

## Execution: How It Works

When you click **Run**, the server:

1. **Validates the graph** — detects cycles, performs topological sort
2. **Loads agents** — reads all `.md` files from `~/.claude/agents/` and project agents
3. **Executes nodes in topological order:**
   - Start node: stores your task as output, no Claude call
   - Agent/Custom node:
     - Collects outputs from all upstream nodes
     - Builds context string (each upstream output labeled by node name)
     - Runs `claude -p "[system prompt + context]"` as subprocess
     - 120-second timeout per node
     - Stores output, emits SSE event → canvas updates live

**Node status on canvas:**
- Gray — not yet run
- Animated purple — currently executing
- Green with checkmark — done
- Red — error or timeout

---

## Context Passing

This is the key mechanism. Each node receives upstream outputs automatically.

**Single upstream (linear chain):**

```
Prompt sent to Node B:
══════════════════════════════
[Node B instructions]

---

## Output from Research:
[Everything Node A returned]

Provide your response:
══════════════════════════════
```

**Multiple upstream (fan-in):**

```
Prompt sent to Node D:
══════════════════════════════
[Node D instructions]

---

## Output from Planner:
[Planner's full output]

## Output from Researcher:
[Researcher's full output]

Provide your response:
══════════════════════════════
```

Node D's Claude call sees both outputs, clearly labeled. It can synthesize, compare, or use them independently.

---

## Building a Pipeline: Step by Step

**Goal: Research → Draft → Polish**

1. Open `/orchestration` → click **New**

2. **Add Start node**
   - Type: Start / Task Input
   - Label: "Task Input"

3. **Add Research node**
   - Type: Agent Node
   - Agent: Nova
   - Label: "Research"
   - Instructions: "Research the given topic. Find competitors, key angles, user pain points. Return structured findings with bullet points. No commentary."
   - Connect: Task Input → Research

4. **Add Draft node**
   - Type: Agent Node
   - Agent: Quill
   - Label: "Draft"
   - Instructions: "Using the research provided, write a complete first draft. Be specific and benefit-focused. Return the draft only — no meta-commentary."
   - Connect: Research → Draft

5. **Add Polish node**
   - Type: Agent Node
   - Agent: Quill
   - Label: "Polish"
   - Instructions: "Polish this draft. Tighten every sentence. Cut filler. Ensure the opening hooks immediately. Return the final polished version only — no commentary."
   - Connect: Draft → Polish

6. **Save:** Click **Save** → name it "Research → Draft → Polish"

7. **Run:** Type task in Run panel → click **Run** → watch live execution

---

## The Run Panel

**Before run:**
- Task input field — type your top-level task
- Run button — starts execution

**During run:**
- Live log — each node completion with first 100 chars of output
- Click "View full output" next to any log entry

**After run:**
- Final Output section — last node's complete response
- Click any green node on canvas to see its full output in the sidebar

**Post-run actions:**
- **Re-run** — same pipeline, same task, fresh execution (useful for getting a variation)
- **Reset** — clears all statuses and outputs, returns to pre-run state

---

## Node Instructions: Bad vs Good

This is the most important thing to get right.

**Bad:**
```
Analyze the research and think about what content would work best.
```
Claude returns commentary about what good content looks like, not the content itself.

**Good:**
```
You are a Shopify app copywriter. Using the research provided:
1. Identify the top 3 user pain points mentioned
2. Write a 5-bullet feature list that directly addresses those pain points
3. Write a 150-word app description

Return only the bullets and description. No commentary, no preamble.
```

**Every node instruction should specify:**
1. What format to return ("Return a bullet list", "Return only the code")
2. What NOT to include ("No commentary", "No preamble")
3. Length or scope ("150 words", "5 bullets", "complete implementation")

**More examples:**

| Bad | Good |
|-----|------|
| "Think about the task and break it down" | "Break the task into 5 numbered implementation steps. Include file names and method names. Return the numbered list only." |
| "Review the code" | "Check for: missing type annotations, `any` usage, unhandled promises. Output: ## Issues Found — [severity] file:line: problem → fix. ## Verdict: PASS / NEEDS FIXES" |
| "Write about the topic" | "Write a 400-word blog intro for: [topic]. Hook in first sentence. Return only the intro text." |

---

## Saving and Loading Pipelines

- **Save:** Click **Save** → enter a name → saved to `orchestrations.json`
- **Load:** Pipelines appear in the left sidebar list — click to load
- **Templates:** Pre-built pipelines at the top of the list — click to load, confirm before replacing canvas
- Saving stores the structure (nodes, edges, instructions) — not previous run outputs

---

## Advanced Patterns

### Fan-Out: Multi-Perspective Analysis

```
Task Input
  → Researcher A: "Find TypeScript/Node solutions"
  → Researcher B: "Find Python solutions"
  → Synthesizer: "Compare both approaches. Recommend best for our stack. Output recommendation only."
  → Developer: "Implement the recommended approach."
```

Both researchers receive only the task. Synthesizer receives both. Developer receives the recommendation.

**Use for:** Architecture decisions, technical comparisons, multi-angle analysis.

### Plan → Implement → Validate

```
Task → Arya (Planner) → Koda (Developer) → Sage (Reviewer)
```

Arya breaks the task into a build plan. Koda implements from the plan. Sage reviews.

**Use for:** Complex feature builds where architecture needs thought before coding.

### Summarizer Node (Controlling Context Size)

Problem: Node 1 returns 8KB of research. Node 2 returns 12KB of code. Node 3 receives 20KB — slow, expensive.

Solution: Summarizer node between heavy-output steps.

```
Research → Summarizer → Developer
```

Summarizer instruction:
```
Condense the above research into 5 key bullet points. Maximum 100 words total.
Preserve the most actionable insights. Return the bullets only.
```

Developer works with 100 words of targeted context instead of 8KB of raw research.

### Validation Gate

```
Task → Developer → Validator
```

Validator instruction:
```
Review the implementation above. Check:
1. Does it follow the project patterns in CLAUDE.md?
2. Are error handling and loading states present?
3. Is input validated with Zod?

Output:
## PASS / FAIL
If FAIL: [issue] → [required fix]
```

If Validator outputs FAIL, re-run with Developer instructions that address the feedback.

### Cascading Specialization

```
Task → Planner → Specialist A (sub-task 1) → Integrator
              → Specialist B (sub-task 2) ↗
```

Planner splits the task. Specialists handle independent parts. Integrator synthesizes.

---

## Performance

| Operation | Typical time |
|-----------|-------------|
| Start/Task node | < 1ms (no Claude call) |
| Simple agent step | 5–20 seconds |
| Complex agent step (full implementation) | 20–60 seconds |
| Full 3-node pipeline | 30–90 seconds |
| Full 5-node pipeline | 75–180 seconds |

Nodes execute sequentially, not in parallel. Each node makes exactly one `claude -p` subprocess call.

**Keep pipelines fast:**
- Add summarizer nodes after heavy-output nodes
- Write focused, specific instructions (specificity = speed + quality)
- 3–5 nodes is the sweet spot; 7+ is usually overkill
- Break one 8-node pipeline into two 4-node pipelines if needed

---

## API Endpoints

| Method | Endpoint | Description |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/api/orchestrations` | List all saved pipelines |
| `POST` | `/api/orchestrations` | Save a pipeline — body: `{ id?, name, nodes, edges }` |
| `GET` | `/api/orchestrations/:id` | Get one saved pipeline |
| `DELETE` | `/api/orchestrations/:id` | Delete a saved pipeline |
| `POST` | `/api/orchestrations/run` | Execute a pipeline with SSE streaming — body: `{ nodes, edges, task }` |

`POST /api/orchestrations/run` returns a Server-Sent Events stream. Each event is a JSON object:

```json
{ "type": "start", "nodeId": "node-1", "label": "Research" }
{ "type": "done", "nodeId": "node-1", "label": "Research", "output": "..." }
{ "type": "complete", "finalOutput": "..." }
{ "type": "error", "nodeId": "node-1", "error": "Timed out after 120s" }
```

---

## Troubleshooting

**Node produces commentary instead of content**
- Cause: Instructions don't specify that Claude should produce the deliverable directly.
- Fix: Add "Return only the [deliverable]. No preamble, no commentary, no explanation."

**Node timeout (120s)**
- Cause: Task scope is too large for one node.
- Fix: Split into two nodes (Plan → Execute). Or narrow the instructions.

**SSE stream drops mid-run / run panel shows nothing**
- Cause: SSE connection broken, often a browser extension or proxy.
- Fix: `pm2 logs claude-hub --lines 30` → check for errors. Then: `pm2 restart claude-hub` and hard-reload the page (Cmd+Shift+R).

**Disconnected node stays gray after run**
- Cause: Node has no incoming edges and is not the Start node.
- Fix: Connect it to an upstream node, or delete it.

**"Circular dependency detected" on run**
- Cause: Nodes form a cycle (A → B → C → A).
- Fix: Find and delete the edge that closes the loop. The system highlights it.

**Pipeline saves but disappears after restart**
- Cause: Write permission issue on `orchestrations.json`.
- Fix:
  ```bash
  chmod 644 "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/orchestrations.json"
  ```

**Pipeline runs but final output is empty**
- Cause: Last node's instructions produce no concrete output, or the node errored silently.
- Fix: Click the last node to inspect its output. Check `pm2 logs claude-hub --lines 50 --err` for subprocess errors.

# Projects & Rules

## What Makes a Project

Claude Hub discovers a directory as a project when it contains at least one of:
- `CLAUDE.md` file
- `.claude/` directory
- `package.json` file
- `pubspec.yaml` file

Hidden directories (starting with `.`) and `node_modules` are skipped automatically.

---

## Adding a New Project

### Step 1: Add the parent directory in Settings

1. Open `http://localhost:3847`
2. Click **Settings**
3. Add: `/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App`
4. Save

Claude Hub scans all subdirectories of configured paths. If your project is inside that folder, it appears automatically.

### Step 2: Create project `CLAUDE.md`

The project-level `CLAUDE.md` at the project root is read by Claude Code whenever that project is open. It supplements the global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` with project-specific context.

**Required sections:**

```markdown
# [Project Name] — [Type: Shopify App / SaaS / API]

## Stack (Exact Versions)
- Framework: [name + version — be exact, not "React 18"]
- UI: [library + version]
- Auth: [how auth works]
- Database: [ORM + DB engine]
- Language: TypeScript strict mode — zero plain .js files
- Node: [minimum version]

## Folder Structure
\`\`\`
[actual top-level directories and key files]
\`\`\`

## Architecture Rules
1. [Rule — be explicit, e.g. "authenticate.admin(request) before every Shopify API call"]
2. ...

## Quality Gates
- npm run typecheck — zero errors
- [project-specific checks]
```

**Stack B (Shopify App) template:**

```markdown
# AppName — Shopify App

## Stack (Exact Versions)
- Framework: React Router 7 (`@shopify/shopify-app-react-router` v1) — NOT Remix
- UI: Shopify Polaris v13 — ONLY Polaris components for admin UI, never raw HTML
- Auth: `shopify.server.ts` → `authenticate.admin(request)` — before every Shopify API call
- Database: Prisma v6 + SQLite (dev) / PostgreSQL (prod)
- Language: TypeScript everywhere
- Node: ≥20

## Architecture Rules
1. Auth first — `authenticate.admin(request)` before any Shopify API usage
2. Loaders/actions only — Shopify API calls ONLY in loaders/actions, never in components
3. Polaris only — ONLY Polaris v13 components inside `app.*` routes
4. DB scoping — every DB query must include `where: { shop: session.shop }`
5. Webhooks — handle idempotently, always return 200

## Quality Gates
- npm run typecheck — zero tolerance for errors
- Every admin route has `authenticate.admin` in both loader and action
- Every DB query has `where: { shop: session.shop }`
- Every list view has EmptyState
- Every form mutation has Toast feedback
```

**Stack A (SaaS) template:**

```markdown
# AppName — SaaS

## Stack (Exact Versions)
- Framework: Next.js 14+ App Router
- UI: Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui
- Auth: Supabase Auth — `createServerClient` server-side, `createBrowserClient` client-side
- Database: Supabase (PostgreSQL) with RLS
- Billing: Stripe subscriptions + webhooks
- Language: TypeScript strict mode
- Deploy: Vercel

## Architecture Rules
1. Server Components by default — `"use client"` only for interactivity or hooks
2. Auth — `getUser()` not `getSession()` on server
3. RLS enabled on ALL tables — default deny
4. API routes — Zod validation on every mutation
5. Error handling — never expose raw Supabase/Stripe errors to client

## Quality Gates
- npm run typecheck — zero errors
- All API routes validate input with Zod
- All mutations have error handling
- Mobile responsive — test at 375px
```

### Step 3: Create the `.claude/` structure

```
YourProject/
  .claude/
    CLAUDE.md        ← project instructions (or at project root)
    agents/          ← project-specific agents (optional)
    commands/        ← slash commands for this project
    rules/           ← hard guardrails (always active)
    settings.json    ← Claude Code permissions config
```

```bash
mkdir -p "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/NewApp/.claude/commands"
mkdir -p "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/NewApp/.claude/agents"
mkdir -p "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/NewApp/.claude/rules"
```

**`settings.json` — required for permissions:**

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run *)",
      "Bash(npx prisma *)",
      "Bash(node *)"
    ],
    "deny": []
  }
}
```

Add `"Bash(npx supabase *)"` for SaaS apps. Adjust based on what Claude Code needs to run without prompting.

### Step 4: Install the SDK

Add to `package.json` `dependencies`:

```json
"@boldteq/agents": "file:../claude-hub/sdk"
```

Then:

```bash
cd "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/NewApp"
npm install
```

Verify:

```bash
node -e "const { isOnline } = require('@boldteq/agents'); isOnline().then(r => console.log('SDK online:', r))"
# Expected: SDK online: true
```

Or use the Claude Hub **Setup** page → Install button to do this automatically.

### Step 5: Verify in Claude Hub

1. Open `http://localhost:3847`
2. Check the project appears in the sidebar or Dashboard
3. Click the project → confirm agents, commands, and rules count correctly

---

## Rules System

### What Rules Are

Rules are hard constraints that Claude must follow in every action within a project. They are always active — Claude reads them automatically before every task.

**Rules vs CLAUDE.md vs Commands:**

| | Rules | CLAUDE.md | Commands |
|--|-------|-----------|----------|
| **Active** | Always — Claude reads automatically | Always — loaded at session start | Only when you type `/name` |
| **Purpose** | Hard guardrails Claude must never break | General guidance, stack info, patterns | Repeatable workflow shortcuts |
| **Tone** | Strict constraint ("Never do X") | Guidance ("Prefer X over Y") | Instructions ("Do X, then Y, then Z") |
| **Location** | `.claude/rules/*.md` | `CLAUDE.md` at root or `.claude/CLAUDE.md` | `.claude/commands/*.md` |

### Where Rules Live

```
YourProject/.claude/rules/
  no-direct-push.md
  zod-validation.md
  no-any.md
  prisma-migrations.md
  no-mock-db.md
```

One rule per file. The filename is the rule name. Plain markdown content — no frontmatter needed.

### Example Rules — Full Content

**`no-direct-push.md`**
```markdown
Never commit or push directly to the main branch.

Always create a feature branch:
- Branch name format: feature/[short-description] or fix/[short-description]
- Example: git checkout -b feature/csv-import

Open a pull request for all changes. Never use git push origin main.
```

**`zod-validation.md`**
```markdown
All API routes must validate request input with Zod schemas. Never trust raw request data.

Required pattern:
\`\`\`typescript
const schema = z.object({ ... })
const result = schema.safeParse(await request.json())
if (!result.success) return Response.json({ error: result.error.flatten() }, { status: 400 })
\`\`\`

Never access `request.json()` fields directly without validation.
Never use `schema.parse()` — always `schema.safeParse()` with explicit error handling.
```

**`no-mock-db.md`**
```markdown
Never mock the database in tests. Always use a real test database with seed data.

Never use: jest.mock('prisma'), vi.mock('@/lib/db'), or any database stub.
Always use: a dedicated test database with DATABASE_URL_TEST in .env.test.

Mocked DB tests give false confidence. Real DB tests catch actual query bugs.
```

**`prisma-migrations.md`**
```markdown
Never modify schema.prisma and apply changes manually in production.

All schema changes must go through:
1. Edit prisma/schema.prisma
2. Run: npx prisma migrate dev --name [descriptive-name]
3. Run: npx prisma generate
4. Commit both the schema change and the migration file

Never run npx prisma db push in production — use migrate deploy.
Never run npx prisma migrate reset without explicit user confirmation — this deletes all data.
```

**`no-any.md`**
```markdown
Never use TypeScript `any` type. No exceptions.

Alternatives:
- Use specific types or interfaces
- Use generics for flexible typing
- Use `unknown` with type guards for truly unknown data
- Use `Parameters<typeof fn>[0]` to infer parameter types

Also forbidden: `as any`, `@ts-ignore`, `@ts-expect-error` (unless the comment explains exactly why and when it will be fixed).
```

### Managing Rules in Claude Hub

- **All Rules page:** `http://localhost:3847/rules` — view all rules across all projects
- **Project detail page:** Click a project in the sidebar → **Rules** tab — create, edit, delete rules for that project
- Rules are stored as `.md` files. Editing via UI writes directly to the file system.

### When to Add a Rule

- Claude repeatedly does something wrong in this project → add a rule stopping it
- A standard is non-negotiable (security, data integrity, billing) → encode it as a rule
- A pattern from CLAUDE.md keeps getting ignored → promote it to a rule

---

## Project Detail Page

**How to access:** Sidebar → click the project name

**What it shows:**
- Project path (absolute)
- CLAUDE.md status (found / not found)
- Agents tab — project-specific agents with edit/create/delete
- Commands tab — slash commands with edit/create/delete
- Rules tab — guardrails with edit/create/delete

Creating or editing any of these via the UI writes directly to the project's `.claude/` directory.

---

## API Endpoints

| Method | Endpoint | Description |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/api/projects` | List all discovered projects |
| `GET` | `/api/projects/:id/claude-md` | Get project CLAUDE.md content |
| `PUT` | `/api/projects/:id/claude-md` | Update project CLAUDE.md |
| `GET` | `/api/projects/:id/agents` | List project agents |
| `GET` | `/api/projects/:id/agents/:name` | Get one project agent |
| `PUT` | `/api/projects/:id/agents/:name` | Create or update project agent |
| `DELETE` | `/api/projects/:id/agents/:name` | Delete project agent |
| `GET` | `/api/projects/:id/commands` | List project commands |
| `GET` | `/api/projects/:id/commands/:name` | Get one command |
| `PUT` | `/api/projects/:id/commands/:name` | Create or update command |
| `DELETE` | `/api/projects/:id/commands/:name` | Delete command |

| `GET` | `/api/projects/:id/rules/:name` | Get one rule |
| `PUT` | `/api/projects/:id/rules/:name` | Create or update rule |
| `DELETE` | `/api/projects/:id/rules/:name` | Delete rule |
| `GET` | `/api/unified/rules` | All rules across all projects |
| `GET` | `/api/unified/commands` | All commands across all projects |
| `GET` | `/api/config` | Current config (project dirs, settings) |
| `POST` | `/api/config/project-dirs` | Update project discovery directories |
| `POST` | `/api/setup/install-sdk` | Install SDK into a project |
| `GET` | `/api/setup/status` | Full setup health check |

`:id` is the base64-encoded project path.

---

## Pre-Build Checklist

```
[ ] CLAUDE.md at project root
    [ ] Stack versions exact (not "React 18" — "React 18.3.1")
    [ ] Architecture rules listed (5–10 rules)
    [ ] Quality gates explicit

[ ] .claude/ directory exists with:

    [ ] CLAUDE.md detected

[ ] Global CLAUDE.md updated:
    [ ] Row added to Active Projects table
```

---

## Troubleshooting
